summary: Suggests a file format for telling multiple mail reading programs about the locally installed facilities for handling mail in various formats, such as MIME types. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A shared settings sheet that tells all your email programs which helper app should open which kind of attachment.

subtitle: A shared configuration file format that tells all mail clients which programs should handle which types of attachments.

tldr.problem: As email moved from plain text to multimedia, different mail reading programs had no common way to know which local programs could display images, audio, video, or other non-text formats, leading to compatibility problems between mail clients.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes a mailcap file format where system administrators list content types and the programs that can handle them, so all mail clients can consult the same configuration to decide how to display attachments.
tldr.outcome: Mailcap became widely used on Unix systems and influenced similar mechanisms on other platforms. It remains part of Unix and Linux distributions today, even though it has been supplemented by MIME type registries and graphical file type associations.

today: Mailcap files remain part of Unix and Linux distributions today. Many programs—mail clients, web browsers, file managers—still use mailcap to determine how to handle different file types. However, mailcap has been supplemented on modern systems by graphical file type associations and MIME type databases. On systems like systemd, MIME types are often configured through mimeapps.list and desktop files, but the underlying concept—a centralized mapping from file types to handler programs—is the same. RFC 1343 is informational but represents a practical, widely-adopted standard for Unix systems.

sections.title: Multimedia Mail and Interoperability
sections.content:
When this RFC was published in June 1992, Internet email was transitioning from plain text only to multimedia messages with multiple content types. The MIME standard (RFC 1341) had just been defined to extend RFC 822 (the email format standard) to support attachments and multiple body parts: images, audio, video, structured data, and more. However, the Internet faced a critical problem: different mail reading programs had no standard way to know what to do with unfamiliar file types. A mail reader that received a JPEG image, an audio file, or a PostScript document had no built-in understanding of how to display it, and each mail client implemented its own proprietary configuration system.

This RFC, authored by Nathaniel Borenstein of Bellcore, proposes a unified configuration mechanism called the mailcap file. The idea is simple but powerful: instead of each mail client inventing its own way to specify external programs for handling content types, all mail clients on a system should read a common configuration file that lists what programs are available locally for displaying each content type. This way, site administrators can add support for new media types in one place, and all mail clients instantly gain that capability.
sections.plainLanguage: When email clients got the ability to handle pictures and other attachments, nobody agreed on how to do it. This standard file format lets everyone use the same configuration so you only have to tell the system once which program handles which kind of file.

sections.title: Mailcap File Format and Fields
sections.content:
A mailcap file is a simple text file with one entry per line, where each entry describes how to handle a MIME content type. Comments start with the hash symbol and blank lines are ignored. Each entry has two required fields: a content-type (like text/plain or image/jpeg) and a view-command (the program that displays that type). The line image/jpeg; /usr/bin/xview %s instructs the system to show JPEG images using xview.

The first field can use wildcard subtypes, such as image/* to match all image types. The second field can include special syntax where %s is replaced by the filename, %t by the content-type, and %{parameter} by values from the Content-Type header. Optional fields come after the semicolon in any order: compose (create that type), edit (modify it), print (output to paper), test (conditional logic), needsterminal (requires a terminal), copiousoutput (produces extensive output), and description (a user-readable label).
sections.plainLanguage: A mailcap file is a list of rules: one line per file type, saying which program should open it. You can add optional fields to control how the program runs.

sections.title: Configuration Hierarchy and Searching
sections.content:
Rather than a single centralized mailcap file, the standard uses a search path of multiple files, allowing both system-wide defaults and per-user overrides. On Unix systems, the RFC recommends searching (in order): the user's home directory ($HOME/.mailcap), then system directories (/etc/mailcap, /usr/etc/mailcap, /usr/local/etc/mailcap). Users can override the entire search path by setting the MAILCAPS environment variable. When a mail client needs to display a content type, it searches through these files in order and uses the first matching entry. An entry matches if: the content-type specification matches the message's type, the entry contains enough information for the application's purpose, and any test field in the entry succeeds (returns exit code zero).

This hierarchy means that a system administrator can set site-wide defaults in /etc/mailcap, and individual users can override them or add local handlers in their home directory's .mailcap file without modifying system files. Different users can have completely different multimedia configurations based on what programs they have installed or prefer to use. The search-first semantics also allow multiple mailcap entries for the same type with different test conditions, so a mail client can use different viewers depending on whether X Windows is running, what audio hardware is present, or other environmental factors.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail programs can have a personal mailcap file in their home folder, and the system has one in a standard place. When displaying a file, it checks the personal one first, then the system one.

sections.title: Composing, Editing, and Advanced Features
sections.content:
Mailcap is not only for viewing; it also supports composing and editing content types. The compose field names a program that can create new messages in a given format. For example, a mail client could offer to let users record audio or draw diagrams by invoking the appropriate composer. The composetyped field is similar but used when the composition program needs to output MIME headers (e.g., for multipart messages where boundary parameters are required). The print field specifies a program for printing a message type to a hardcopy device.

The test field is particularly powerful: it allows a mailcap entry to apply conditionally. For instance, an audio/* entry might be enabled only on machines with audio hardware. The test field contains a program that returns zero (true) or non-zero (false). If a test fails, the mail client continues searching for the next mailcap entry, allowing fallback behavior. The needsterminal flag tells graphical mail clients that the command requires an interactive terminal window; window managers can create one if needed. The copiousoutput flag indicates that the command produces many lines of output, so the mail client should page or scroll it rather than letting it flood the display. Together, these features allow mailcap to express sophisticated, context-dependent handling of multimedia content.
sections.plainLanguage: You can also tell the system how to compose or print different types. And you can say "only use this if audio hardware is present" or "this program needs a terminal window."

sections.title: Real-World Usage and Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC includes a sample mailcap file demonstrating typical usage. One entry sends richtext format to a richtext display program with output paging: text/richtext; richtext %s; copiousoutput. Another plays audio files only if the system has audio hardware: audio/*; showaudio; test=/usr/local/bin/hasaudio. A complex example handles Andrew format email using the Andrew System's tools: x-be2; /usr/andrew/bin/ezview %s; print=...; compose=...; copiousoutput. Mail clients use these entries to invoke the right program when displaying a message, passing the attachment content as standard input or via a temporary file depending on whether %s appears in the command.

The RFC's design is extensible. Fields beginning with x- are reserved for local or vendor-specific extensions; implementations should ignore unrecognized fields. This allows mailcap to be extended on a per-site or per-vendor basis without breaking compatibility. The RFC also discusses, in Appendix C, the idea of using mailcap-like mechanisms for format translation—chaining multiple programs to convert one format to another—but deliberately keeps the core mechanism simple and focused on a single-line lookup model rather than building a complex pipeline system into the standard.
sections.plainLanguage: You can build complex rules: "show X if this test passes, otherwise try the next entry." And vendors can add their own special fields without breaking other programs.

fields.name: Content-Type
fields.desc: MIME type, e.g. text/plain or image/*

fields.name: View Command
fields.desc: Program to display the type, with %s for filename
